shots.B13C168S18H01: Footnote 69 explains tadarpani as the one who attains your form.
shots.B13C168S18H02: Footnote 70 explains kriti and vikara and compares the variant readings pralaya and pranaya, and glosses prabhava as sovereignty.
shots.B13C168S18H03: Footnote 71 says the ganas are the principles that are counted.
shots.B13C168S18H04: Footnote 72 says the heavenly felicity won by righteous acts is Mahadeva, and that acts unfold in time marked by the sun.
shots.B13C168S18H05: Footnote 73 notes that Yogins could create worlds by their power but refrain out of respect for the Grandsire.
shots.B13C168S19H01: Footnote 74 contrasts the Bengal reading satyasandhah with the Bombay satrasatwah, meaning firm resolve.
shots.B13C168S19H02: Footnote 75 glosses vigraham as a form of special power, or as pure knowledge.
shots.B13C168S19H03: Footnote 76 notes Upamanyu's promise of sixteen and eight boons and says the commentator's count is strained.
shots.B13C168S19H04: Footnote 77 glosses an address to Ganga as the cleanser of all cleansing things.
shots.B13C168S19H05: Footnote 78 explains the six divisions of self and world: the adhyatma, adhibhuta, adhidaivata, adhiloka, adhivijnana and adhiyajna.
shots.B13C168S20H01: Footnote 79 says the liberated attain emancipation by seeing Mahadeva in the firmament of their hearts or by uniting their souls with him.
shots.B13C168S20H02: Footnote 80 says the cave where Brahman is hidden is the heart of every creature.
shots.B13C168S20H03: Footnote 81 lists the worlds and the eight forms of Mahadeva, with their names, and cites Kalidasa's Shakuntala.
shots.B13C168S20H04: Footnote 82 says the cave of the scriptures, perhaps meaning difficult texts, is where Mahadeva is hidden.
shots.B13C168S20H05: Footnote 83 says these people need no extraordinary effort, since their devotion alone draws Mahadeva to them.
shots.B13C168S21H01: Footnote 84 explains the Devayana and Pitriyana, the paths of the departed to the sun and to the moon.
shots.B13C168S21H02: Footnote 85 lists the three ways of worship: that of the Srutis, that of the Smritis, and that of meditation.
shots.B13C168S21H03: Footnote 86 refers to the Sankhya Karika for the seven principles beginning with Mahat and Ahankara.
shots.B13C168S21H04: Footnote 87 says the earlier translators misrender the last verse, and explains Devesah as Brahma, who gave the secret names.
shots.B13C168S21H05: Footnote 88 says that reciting these names destroys all fear and the Rakshasas, who flee or die at their sound.
shots.B13C168S22H01: Footnote 89 says the name has the merit of meditation or yoga.
shots.B13C168S22H02: Footnote 90 says sthira and sthanu both imply immutability.
shots.B13C168S22H03: Footnote 91 explains bhava as that from which all things arise and into which they merge, or pure existence.
shots.B13C168S22H04: Footnote 92 glosses a name as Virat, meaning vast or infinite.
shots.B13C168S22H05: Footnote 93 says many names bear several senses, and explains niyata as an ascetic and smasanu as a crematorium or Varanasi.
shots.B13C168S23H01: Footnote 94 gives an alternative sense: the universe is displayed in him.
shots.B13C168S23H02: Footnote 95 says Mahadeva is probably the inner soul free from ignorance.
shots.B13C168S23H03: Footnote 96 explains niyama as inner and outer purity, contentment, austerity and study.
shots.B13C168S23H04: Footnote 97 explains nidhi as the largest named number, implying inexhaustible felicity.
shots.B13C168S23H05: Footnote 98 explains sahasraksha as Indra or the many-eyed, visalaksha as far-seeing, and soma as the moon or the sacrificial juice.
shots.B13C168S24H01: Footnote 99 explains the astronomical names Ketu, Rahu, Mangala, Brihaspati, Sukra, Budha and Durvasa's descent from Atri's wife.
shots.B13C168S24H02: Footnote 100 explains suvarna-retas as Mahadeva's seed becoming a golden egg, or as the deity of fire.
shots.B13C168S24H03: Footnote 101 says the soul carries its seed of acts, ignorance and desire, as a rider is carried by a car.
shots.B13C168S24H04: Footnote 102 identifies Ganapati as Ganesa and the Ganas as Mahadeva's attendants.
shots.B13C168S24H05: Footnote 103 explains digvasas as nude, but says the true sense is that Mahadeva's covering is empty space.
shots.B13C168S25H01: Footnote 104 says that with Mahadeva knowledge serves as penance, in place of bodily austerity.
shots.B13C168S25H02: Footnote 105 explains sataghni as a weapon that kills a hundred, perhaps a kind of rocket.
shots.B13C168S25H03: Footnote 106 explains Harikesa as one whose senses are his rays, through which the mind gains knowledge.
shots.B13C168S25H04: Footnote 107 explains Krishna through the root for existence and the letter for release, giving a sense of pure bliss.
shots.B13C168S25H05: Footnote 108 explains Kaparddin by the story of Ganga caught in Mahadeva's matted locks, and by the word for lordship.
shots.B13C168S26H01: Footnote 109 says space is Mahadeva's abode, and that the Bengal reading Nabhastala is faulty.
shots.B13C168S26H02: Footnote 110 says the deities move by day and the Asuras and Rakshasas by night, so Mahadeva is both friend and foe of them.
shots.B13C168S26H03: Footnote 111 says unmanifest sound lies in the womb of space and is the unstruck sound of Brahman.
shots.B13C168S26H04: Footnote 112 lists the four states as Visva, Taijasa, Prajna and Sivadhyana, following the commentator.
shots.B13C168S26H05: Footnote 113 offers an alternative sense that Mahadeva is the Buddha who preached against sacrifices.
shots.B13C168S27H05: Footnote 118 explains the three names as householder, sanyasin and forest recluse, each marked by a different hairstyle.
shots.B13C168S28H01: Footnote 119 says Brahman is felt in the firmament of the heart, so Mahadeva appears as light within each body.
shots.B13C168S28H02: Footnote 120 explains kalakatankatah as Yama covered by the Supreme Deity's illusion, which the Supreme Deity also covers.
shots.B13C168S28H03: Footnote 121 says vibhaga and sarvaga mean that the universe is both individual and whole.
shots.B13C168S28H04: Footnote 122 notes that some editions read susaranab, meaning protector of the universe.
shots.B13C168S28H05: Footnote 123 explains the golden mail as the Supreme Deity's illusion, through which the universe is displayed.
shots.B13C168S29H01: Footnote 124 glosses Pasupati as the lord of beasts that need a goad.
shots.B13C168S29H02: Footnote 125 explains tarangavit as one who knows worldly joys, which rise and fall like waves on the sea of eternity.
shots.B13C168S29H03: Footnote 126 identifies the binder of Asura chiefs as the Vishnu form that bound Vali, and notes the plural for successive Kalpas.
shots.B13C168S29H04: Footnote 127 says Mahadeva is well versed in the rituals of sacrifice.
shots.B13C168S29H05: Footnote 128 offers the alternative that Mahadeva needs no vestments, since none could cover his vast limbs.
shots.B13C168S30H01: Footnote 129 says the supporters of the world are the elephants of the quarters and Sesha, and that Mahadeva is the best of them.
shots.B13C168S30H02: Footnote 130 says Mahadeva is Vishnu, the foremost of the celestials, and Agni, the lowest of them, so all of them.
shots.B13C168S30H03: Footnote 131 calls the body a pit into which the soul falls, drawn down by desire and ignorance.
shots.B13C168S30H04: Footnote 132 explains Vasu as the wind, which settles all things into itself.
shots.B13C168S30H05: Footnote 133 explains nisachara as one who lives by night, meaning the soul held by ignorance.
shots.B13C168S31H01: Footnote 134 says the soul can see itself when it rises above the body through yoga.
shots.B13C168S31H02: Footnote 135 says the two words mean Hansa and Paramahansa.
shots.B13C168S31H03: Footnote 136 explains varhaspatya as a word for a priest, derived from Vrihaspati.
shots.B13C168S31H04: Footnote 137 says the name Nandivardhana may also mean one who takes away joy already given.
shots.B13C168S31H05: Footnote 138 notes that the language of the Veda is divine and that of the scriptures is human.
shots.B13C168S32H01: Footnote 139 says the phrase means the crown of the head.
shots.B13C168S32H02: Footnote 140 says the phrase means one who wins his own emancipation.
shots.B13C168S32H03: Footnote 141 identifies Mahanakha with the Man-lion avatar and Maharoman with the Boar avatar.
shots.B13C168S32H04: Footnote 142 explains Mahamuni as one who reflects deeply or who is very taciturn.
shots.B13C168S32H05: Footnote 143 refers the reader to the Moksha sections of the Santi Parva on the world as a tree.
shots.B13C168S33H01: Footnote 144 says no one can inquire after Brahman without a body and senses, and that the tree of the world is evidence of the Supreme Deity.
shots.B13C168S33H02: Footnote 145 faults both earlier translators for misreading names such as Yaju and Padabhuja.
shots.B13C168S33H03: Footnote 146 lists the ten stages of life, from the mother's womb to death, with heaven as the eleventh and emancipation as the twelfth.
shots.B13C168S33H04: Footnote 147 says Kali, though an age of sin, makes emancipation quick for those who live righteously.
shots.B13C168S33H05: Footnote 148 says Mahadeva takes the form of the Great Bear, called Sisumara by Hindu astronomers because it looks like a tortoise.
shots.B13C168S34H01: Footnote 149 explains bhashma as anything that dispels bonds and disease, and why ascetics rub it on their bodies.
shots.B13C168S34H02: Footnote 150 says Mahadeva gave ashes to his devotees to protect them from sin.
shots.B13C168S34H03: Footnote 151 tells the story of the sage Mankanaka, whose dance led Mahadeva to show ashes from his body.
shots.B13C168S34H04: Footnote 152 explains anukari as an accessory, the Supreme Deity acting as Krishna to aid Arjuna in slaying Bhishma.
shots.B13C168S34H05: Footnote 153 says the phrase refers to Krishna as Arjuna's friend.
shots.B13C168S35H01: Footnote 154 says the snake Sesha, who holds up the earth in the myths, is Mahadeva, also called Ananta.
shots.B13C168S35H02: Footnote 155 identifies Mahavishnu as the god from whose navel the lotus of Brahma arose.
shots.B13C168S35H03: Footnote 156 notes a misprint in the Bombay text, Punya-chanchu for Punya-chunchu, which the Burdwan translation repeats.
shots.B13C168S35H04: Footnote 157 explains Kurukshetra as the field of action and the field where King Kuru did penance, sacred even in its dust.
shots.B13C168S35H05: Footnote 158 says Siddharthah means Siddhanta, with the following compound as its adjective.
shots.B13C168S36H01: Footnote 159 says the phrase means the soul of real existence.
shots.B13C168S36H02: Footnote 160 explains Mahadeva's plate as Kala, the destroyer, and notes errors in the earlier translations.
shots.B13C168S36H03: Footnote 161 says Mahadeva is the foremost of worshippers, having reduced all passions to nothing.
shots.B13C168S36H04: Footnote 162 gives the commentator's explanation of the name Narah.
shots.B13C168S36H05: Footnote 163 says the one called Suparvan in heaven is also called Mahan.
shots.B13C168S37H01: Footnote 164 explains the name as one who gives the power to bear all griefs and joys without losing life.
shots.B13C168S37H02: Footnote 165 calls the commentator's etymology of Hara fanciful.
shots.B13C168S37H03: Footnote 166 explains a nipana as a shallow pond where cattle drink, so that the oceans are Mahadeva.
shots.B13C168S37H04: Footnote 167 links the phrase to Trivikrama, the dwarf who grew to cover heaven and earth with two steps.
shots.B13C168S37H05: Footnote 168 says the phrase means one possessed of Yoga knowledge.
shots.B13C168S38H01: Footnote 169 says two words together form one name.
shots.B13C168S38H02: Footnote 170 names vija, sakti and kilakani, and explains a kakud as a hump.
shots.B13C168S38H03: Footnote 171 says the Brahmana's thin rod is mightier than Indra's thunderbolt, and that its might comes from Mahadeva.
shots.B13C168S38H04: Footnote 172 explains the compound Sayambhuva Tigmatejah, since Brahman could not look at Mahadeva.
shots.B13C168S38H05: Footnote 173 says Brahma's fruitless search for the end of the lotus stalk implies that Mahadeva is infinite.
shots.B13C168S39H01: Footnote 174 tells how Surabhi bore false witness for Brahma and was cursed by Siva.
shots.B13C168S39H02: Footnote 175 says Uma is another name for Brahmavidya.
shots.B13C168S39H03: Footnote 176 tells how Mahadeva held Ganga in his matted locks and let her flow to the sea over the ashes of Sagara's sons.
shots.B13C168S39H04: Footnote 177 refers back to the Hara-Gauri form.
shots.B13C168S39H05: Footnote 178 notes the variant readings Pritatma and Pitatma.
shots.B13C168S40H01: Footnote 179 says Mahadeva has five heads, four on the sides and one above.
shots.B13C168S40H02: Footnote 180 says the phrase amritogovrisherwarah is a single name.
shots.B13C168S40H03: Footnote 181 says these are names for different portions of time.
shots.B13C168S40H04: Footnote 182 quotes the Srutis that make fire his head and the sun and moon his eyes.
shots.B13C168S40H05: Footnote 183 says a shrine called Vyaghreswara in the Kalinga country is dedicated to him.
shots.B13C168S41H01: Footnote 184 explains kanta as the limit of happiness.
shots.B13C168S41H02: Footnote 185 says devotion to Bhava requires knowing every mode of worship and special good luck.
shots.B13C168S41H03: Footnote 186 notes that the gods sent nymphs to tempt men whose penances alarmed them.
shots.B13C168S41H04: Footnote 187 says the translator expands a verse to make its sense plain.
shots.B13C168S41H05: Footnote 188 explains Yudhishthira's objection that a joint religious union cannot last past death, and that partners pursue different ends.
shots.B13C168S42H01: Footnote 189 explains that the journey is a test the groom must pass before claiming his bride.
shots.B13C168S42H02: Footnote 190 defines Kala-ratri as the night before the universal dissolution.
shots.B13C168S42H03: Footnote 191 says the commentator takes uttaram to mean the sacred north.
shots.B13C168S42H04: Footnote 192 says tirtha here means a ghat, an easy descent to the water.
shots.B13C168S42H05: Footnote 193 says pradhanatah means with the foremost Vedic mantras.
shots.B13C168S43H01: Footnote 194 explains Mandakini as the part of the Ganga that flows through Kailasa and Nalini as a lotus lake of the Yaksha king.
shots.B13C168S43H02: Footnote 195 says divya means excellent Gandharva music and dance.
shots.B13C168S43H03: Footnote 196 says a woman is said to destroy a family by unchastity.
shots.B13C168S43H04: Footnote 197 says the translators misread the second line, which means the sage does not yet yearn for her company.
shots.B13C168S43H05: Footnote 198 says the commentator takes utsaditah to mean shaken, a sense the translator doubts here.
shots.B13C168S44H01: Footnote 199 offers an alternative sense: go to your own bed and rest alone.
shots.B13C168S44H02: Footnote 200 calls the commentator's reading of a choice between two women far-fetched.
shots.B13C168S44H03: Footnote 201 explains sakti and dhriti in a verse and faults the earlier translators' rendering.
shots.B13C168S44H04: Footnote 202 explains lingin and alingin, meaning those with and without the marks of their order, and the question of who is worthy of gifts.
shots.B13C168S44H05: Footnote 203 says the competence of Brahmanas should be examined in acts done for the Pitris.
shots.B13C168S45H01: Footnote 204 says the question names five persons, and explains sambandhi as relatives by marriage.
shots.B13C168S45H02: Footnote 205 says a Brahmana who keeps three acts is free from sin, and that these refer to birth and knowledge.
shots.B13C168S45H03: Footnote 206 says good conduct means modesty and candour.
shots.B13C168S45H04: Footnote 207 explains anekantam as yielding many kinds of fruit, since the objects of duty vary.
shots.B13C168S45H05: Footnote 208 explains the four genitive nouns of verse 22 for the outcasts of towns and gossips who expose others, and questions the translations.
shots.B13C168S46H01: Footnote 209 prefers the Bengal reading brahmacharyya and explains maryyada as the limits of duty.
shots.B13C168S46H02: Footnote 210 says a gift to even one such Brahmana rescues the ancestors and descendants of the giver.
shots.B13C168S46H03: Footnote 211 says gifts must suit their time, since untimely gifts go to Rakshasas.
shots.B13C168S46H04: Footnote 212 says food partly eaten by unworthy persons goes to Rakshasas, and one unable to utter Om is a Sudra.
shots.B13C168S46H05: Footnote 213 notes that the speaker names the unworthy first in order to point out the worthy.
shots.B13C168S47H01: Footnote 214 explains apasmara as a kind of epilepsy in which the sufferer imagines a monster before him.
shots.B13C168S47H02: Footnote 215 explains agrani as the Brahmana who receives the first Sraddha food for the departed, and says he is regarded as fallen.
shots.B13C168S47H03: Footnote 216 says Brahmanas who assist the rites at crematoria are regarded as fallen.
shots.B13C168S47H04: Footnote 217 explains putrika-putra as a son born of a daughter who is counted as the daughter's father's son.
shots.B13C168S47H05: Footnote 218 explains anugraham as the merit that neutralises faults.
shots.B13C168S48H01: Footnote 219 gives Drona, Ashwatthama, Kripa and Rama as examples of the category.
shots.B13C168S48H02: Footnote 220 explains uditastamita as one who spends all his wealth on gifts, and astamitodita as one who grows rich and spends on good ends.
shots.B13C168S48H03: Footnote 221 says the officiating Brahmana declares a Sraddha well performed, a custom still kept.
shots.B13C168S48H04: Footnote 222 says the translator wrongly renders somakshaya as somarasah.
shots.B13C168S48H05: Footnote 223 explains punyaham as the sacred day, with the reply given at the close of rites.
shots.B13C168S49H01: Footnote 224 says slaughter in sacrifice brings no sin, but killing animals for food alone does.
shots.B13C168S49H02: Footnote 225 explains impurity after births and deaths among close kin, and its length for Brahmanas.
shots.B13C168S49H03: Footnote 226 says begging under false pretences, such as a pilgrimage or a son's thread ceremony, is sinful.
shots.B13C168S49H04: Footnote 227 explains that the phrase means those who have suffered at the hands of thieves and still tremble.
shots.B13C168S49H05: Footnote 228 defends the view that a lie may be honourable in some cases, such as to save life or property or to shield a woman's honour.
shots.B13C168S50H01: Footnote 229 says selling the Vedas means charging fees to teach them, and that writing them down was seen as wrong.
shots.B13C168S50H02: Footnote 230 says paying for a poor man's marriage to a good girl is an act of righteousness, with property given to support the couple.
shots.B13C168S50H03: Footnote 231 says the articles needed in marriage are the bride and her ornaments.
shots.B13C168S50H04: Footnote 232 says vapra probably means a field enclosed by ditches and causeways.
shots.B13C168S50H05: Footnote 233 identifies the ancient Chandrabhaga with the Chenab and Vitasta with the Jhelum.
shots.B13C168S51H01: Footnote 234 says one goes to the Apsaras' region and is honoured there.
shots.B13C168S51H02: Footnote 235 says the phrase means one gains sovereignty.
shots.B13C168S51H03: Footnote 236 finds the connection of the second line of a verse hard to follow, and notes that human sacrifices were once made.
shots.B13C168S51H04: Footnote 237 says nyastani takes Gangayam as understood after it.
shots.B13C168S51H05: Footnote 238 says the gods live on offerings from the earth and the cow, which the Asuras harmed by killing kine.
shots.B13C168S52H01: Footnote 239 says the Ganga has three courses: Bhagirathi on earth, Mandakini in heaven, and Bhogabati in the nether regions.
shots.B13C168S52H02: Footnote 240 says Devesh means lord of the deities, but here means emperor.
shots.B13C168S52H03: Footnote 241 explains aranyaih as courses of conduct that lead to Brahmaloka.
shots.B13C168S52H04: Footnote 242 retells how Kapila burned Sagara's sixty thousand sons and how Bhagiratha brought Ganga down to redeem them.
shots.B13C168S52H05: Footnote 243 says the phrase means identical with the universe, and that vrihati means foremost.
shots.B13C168S53H01: Footnote 244 explains madhumatim as conferring the fruits of all good acts.
shots.B13C168S53H02: Footnote 245 explains viswam avanti, with the missing number treated as an arsha form.
shots.B13C168S53H04: Footnote 247 says the construction of the verse is not difficult, though both earlier translations misread it.
shots.B13C168S53H05: Footnote 248 says the Brahmana grants others' desires and creates what he himself wants, through his power and kindness.
shots.B13C168S54H01: Footnote 249 explains ekaramah as one who delights in himself and depends on no one for joy.
shots.B13C168S54H02: Footnote 250 explains dasatirdasa as ten times a hundred, like the other numerals in -ty, and says the earlier translators erred.
shots.B13C168S54H03: Footnote 251 gives the grammar of a Sanskrit phrase about Brahmanas, as the commentator explains it.
shots.B13C168S54H04: Footnote 252 says yajanti means worship with reference to truth and righteousness, and giving with reference to land and kine.
shots.B13C168S54H05: Footnote 253 explains that pigeons pick up scattered grain, a practice recommended in the Sila and other vows.
shots.B13C168S55H01: Footnote 254 explains the aggregate of three as Righteousness, Wealth and Pleasure, kept in view in all acts.
shots.B13C168S55H02: Footnote 255 notes a variant that would have kings honour aged Brahmanas learned in the Vedas.
shots.B13C168S55H03: Footnote 256 says Brahmanas take up many occupations to conceal their true nature or to protect the world.
shots.B13C168S55H04: Footnote 257 says food given to a Brahmana is really eaten by the deities.
shots.B13C168S55H05: Footnote 258 glosses bhutatmanah as those who have mastered the elements.
shots.B13C168S56H01: Footnote 259 calls the second line of verse 18 a crux, and the footnote itself breaks off mid-word.
shots.B13C168S56H02: Footnote 260 says the dark spots on the moon came from Daksha's curse, and the ocean's saltiness from a sage's curse.
shots.B13C168S56H03: Footnote 261 says Brahmana status comes by birth alone, and that a Brahmana has the first share of cooked food.
shots.B13C168S56H04: Footnote 262 says saudram karma refers to serving others, which is forbidden to Brahmanas.
shots.B13C168S56H05: Footnote 263 says a good Brahmana may take precedence even over children at food prepared for guests.
shots.B13C168S57H01: Footnote 264 says Brahmanas who refuse gifts are superior and powerful, and notes that the translator misreads the second line.
shots.B13C168S57H02: Footnote 265 gives the grammar of a verse on the teaching that comes from the Brahmana's mouth, and says both translations err.
shots.B13C168S57H03: Footnote 266 says Sukra aided the Asuras and Vrihaspati the deities with Mantras, which shows Brahmana power.
shots.B13C168S57H04: Footnote 267 says bhumireto is a misprint for bhumiretau, and that the translator makes nonsense of it.
shots.B13C168S57H05: Footnote 268 expands a verse on the many objects of alms-seeking and the silent vow of wandering.
shots.B13C168S58H01: Footnote 269 says undeserving people feel grief at receiving gifts, and that Yudhishthira asks who is worthy.
shots.B13C168S58H02: Footnote 270 says rites must be done with pure intention, so sacrifices should not be made in pride.
shots.B13C168S58H03: Footnote 271 says words and women are both unseizable and hard to understand.
shots.B13C168S58H04: Footnote 272 says women stir the hearts of those who honour them and those who scorn them alike.
shots.B13C168S58H05: Footnote 273 says all living creatures are virtuous, since they can progress toward godship by their acts.
shots.B13C168S59H01: Footnote 274 says pura means first here, in the sense that the speaker comes to the listener first.
shots.B13C168S59H02: Footnote 275 says ladies spoke Prakrit, not Sanskrit, so Indra is surprised to hear refined Sanskrit from a woman.
shots.B13C168S59H03: Footnote 276 explains the adana rite, in which kinsmen made gifts, and lists similar rites such as the sacred thread and marriage.
shots.B13C168S59H04: Footnote 277 says the commentator tries to fit five forms into Manu's eight, and argues that this passage of the Mahabharata is older than Manu.
shots.B13C168S59H05: Footnote 278 says that in ancient times children of Brahmana, Kshatriya or Vaisya mothers had the same status.
shots.B13C168S60H01: Footnote 279 explains nagnika as a girl wearing a single cloth, a reference to the rule about girls of ten.
shots.B13C168S60H02: Footnote 280 explains the putrikadharmini, a daughter married on the understanding that her son will belong to her father.
shots.B13C168S60H03: Footnote 281 refers readers to works on Hindu law for the terms sapinda and sagotra.
shots.B13C168S60H04: Footnote 282 explains the terse verses on when sin attaches to giving a girl in marriage, and when the marriage is complete.
shots.B13C168S60H05: Footnote 283 says that a girl promised to one man may give him up and marry another.
shots.B13C168S61H01: Footnote 284 says that by the boon no sin attaches to retracting a promise to give a daughter for a more eligible husband.
shots.B13C168S61H02: Footnote 285 advises against giving a daughter to an ineligible man, since the offspring cannot be good.
shots.B13C168S61H03: Footnote 286 explains the circumambulation rite and the water and kusa grass used when gifts are made.
shots.B13C168S61H04: Footnote 287 says Savitri's act at her father's bidding was not against duty, and faults two translations of the verse.
shots.B13C168S61H05: Footnote 288 says the grant of liberty to women is an Asura practice, against the true Aryan usage.
shots.B13C168S62H01: Footnote 289 says marriage should not be led by desire alone, nor should the maiden choose for herself under carnal motives.
shots.B13C168S62H02: Footnote 290 says property is divided into five parts, two for the daughter and three for the son.
shots.B13C168S62H03: Footnote 291 says the verse is expanded with the reasons Hindu lawyers give.
shots.B13C168S62H04: Footnote 292 says the condemnation covers only forced consent, so Krishna's abduction of Rukmini and Arjuna's of Subhadra are excluded.
shots.B13C168S62H05: Footnote 293 says a maiden may accept ornaments without turning the marriage into a sale.
shots.B13C168S63H01: Footnote 294 explains swalpa-kaupinah as one covered by a small cloth, and so easily seduced.
shots.B13C168S63H02: Footnote 295 says a Brahmana should not hoard wealth but use it for sacrifice, gifts and his household.
shots.B13C168S63H03: Footnote 296 says a Brahmana who favours wives of other orders over his own becomes like a Chandala among Brahmanas.
shots.B13C168S63H04: Footnote 297 explains how property divides among the sons of three Brahmana wives, and disputes a Bengal argument against more than one wife in one's order.
shots.B13C168S63H05: Footnote 298 says each order was made for sacrifice, and the Sudra's part is to serve the three others in their sacrifices.
shots.B13C168S64H01: Footnote 299 says that some men are not invested with the sacred thread.
shots.B13C168S64H02: Footnote 300 says broken pots are cast off, though lower castes sometimes use them.
shots.B13C168S64H03: Footnote 301 explains that one of low birth stays low in disposition, and that goodness shows itself in acts according to a man's place.
shots.B13C168S64H04: Footnote 302 says a son born after marriage to a man who is not the husband belongs to the husband.
shots.B13C168S64H05: Footnote 303 says such a son belongs to the mother's husband unless the begetter wishes to claim and rear him.
shots.B13C168S65H01: Footnote 304 says the aim of Yudhishthira's question will become clear in Bhishma's answer.
shots.B13C168S65H02: Footnote 305 says the cow is regarded as sanctifying, and that her dung and urine are efficient disinfectants.
shots.B13C168S65H03: Footnote 306 says two good persons who speak seven words or walk seven steps together become friends.
shots.B13C168S65H04: Footnote 307 says vajrasuchyagram may also mean having an end like the needle used to bore diamonds.
shots.B13C168S65H05: Footnote 308 says the shifting evening clouds are regarded as the mansions of the Gandharvas.
shots.B13C168S66H01: Footnote 309 gives botanical names for a long list of trees and creepers, including mango, Asoka, champaka and jack-fruit.
shots.B13C168S66H02: Footnote 310 identifies the birds named in the verse, including the koel, woodpecker, lapwing, partridge, crane and brahminy duck.
shots.B13C168S66H03: Footnote 311 corrects asmi and tapacchaitat in verses 39 and 40 to asi and tapasaccha.
shots.B13C168S66H04: Footnote 312 explains the allusion to a Kshatriya born in Bhrigu's race and the stain passed to it from Kusika's line.
shots.B13C168S66H05: Footnote 313 says Kusika wishes to know which descendant of Bhrigu will confer this honour on his family.
shots.B13C168S67H01: Footnote 314 says the phrase covers ancestors and descendants to the seventh degree.
shots.B13C168S67H02: Footnote 315 says heaven and hell are places of enjoyment and suffering only, while this world is the field of acts.
shots.B13C168S67H03: Footnote 316 defines the Sanskrit names for trees, shrubs, creepers, bamboo and grass.
shots.B13C168S67H04: Footnote 317 explains Yudhishthira's question: giver and receiver do not meet in the next world, so how could a gift come back?
shots.B13C168S67H05: Footnote 318 says the commentator understands abhimanat in a different way.
shots.B13C168S68H01: Footnote 319 prefers the reading yuktaih and glosses the phrase about men charged with a commission.
shots.B13C168S68H02: Footnote 320 says the sacrifice meant is the sacrifice of gifts, with its articles set out in order.
shots.B13C168S68H03: Footnote 321 says gifts to such Brahmanas free the giver from his debts to the gods, and explains the water of gifts.
shots.B13C168S68H04: Footnote 322 explains that heaven and hell both come through the Brahmanas, who grant heaven when pleased and hurl one into hell when angry.
shots.B13C168S68H05: Footnote 323 glosses words for begging and says the Santi passage on driving away beggars applies only to professionals.
shots.B13C168S69H01: Footnote 324 explains antarvedyan as within the platform and anrisamsyatah as outside it.
shots.B13C168S69H02: Footnote 325 says sacrifices are a means of giving to Brahmanas.
shots.B13C168S69H03: Footnote 326 says weeping women are destitute and unable to pay.
shots.B13C168S69H04: Footnote 327 corrects the first word of a line from kshatam to kritam.
shots.B13C168S69H05: Footnote 328 says that a gift from one who is dear to one who is dear is why the woman is called Priyadatta.
shots.B13C168S70H01: Footnote 329 calls the verse a crux, since praise here may mean censure, and suggests another reading.
shots.B13C168S70H02: Footnote 330 says this is the declaration of the earth herself.
shots.B13C168S70H03: Footnote 331 explains the six tastes as drawn from the soil, since the same earth grows sugarcane and tamarind.
shots.B13C168S70H05: Footnote 333 prefers the Bombay reading adityatastansha to the Bengal one.
shots.B13C168S71H01: Footnote 334 says Yudhishthira wishes to know which occasions suit which gifts.
shots.B13C168S71H02: Footnote 335 defines payasa as rice boiled in sweetened milk, a pleasant liquid food.
shots.B13C168S71H03: Footnote 336 names vardhamana, sarava or saravika as a flat cup or dish.
shots.B13C168S71H04: Footnote 337 defines phanita as thickened sugarcane juice.
shots.B13C168S71H05: Footnote 338 defines prasanga as a bamboo or similar basket for covering paddy.
shots.B13C168S72H01: Footnote 339 identifies rajamasha as a kind of bean, Vigna sinensis.
shots.B13C168S72H02: Footnote 340 explains acts done with and without desire for fruit, and says a sesame Sraddha should never be done without it.
shots.B13C168S72H03: Footnote 341 says a giver who gives a house to a Brahmana who lives in it earns the stated reward, which differs from simple hospitality.
shots.B13C168S72H04: Footnote 342 notes that in Bengal tenants seek the landlord's leave before a Sraddha, and that a royal fee is payable.
shots.B13C168S73H01: Footnote 344 explains kinasa as a tiller or a cattle-slayer, and suggests that kasai, the butcher, is a corruption of it.
shots.B13C168S73H02: Footnote 345 says one need dedicate only what one eats, citing Rama's offering in exile, and notes that Pisachas offer carrion.
shots.B13C168S73H03: Footnote 346 glosses the terse verse on time, which says the speaker cannot let these things stay unbidden.
shots.B13C168S73H04: Footnote 347 says Brahmanas should be invited to feasts where sesame predominates.
shots.B13C168S73H05: Footnote 348 describes shaded resting places set up in Bengal in the hot month of Vaisakha, with water, grain and raw sugar for travellers.
shots.B13C168S74H01: Footnote 349 explains the gift of lamps as placing them in dark places, such as roads and ghats.
shots.B13C168S74H02: Footnote 350 says the word of equal name links cow, earth and speech.
shots.B13C168S74H03: Footnote 351 says the number meant is not fixed but means innumerable.
shots.B13C168S74H04: Footnote 352 says hence refers to what was said earlier about kine.
shots.B13C168S74H05: Footnote 353 gives a grammatical note on vitasokaih, which may refer to Bhavanaih or Lokah.
shots.B13C168S75H01: Footnote 354 says only good kine, not lean animals, should be given to Brahmanas.
shots.B13C168S75H02: Footnote 355 says kine feed sacrifice with ghee, which sustains the gods who send rain and crops.
shots.B13C168S75H03: Footnote 356 says the Rishis understood that heat is the source of the growth of many things.
shots.B13C168S75H04: Footnote 357 says a preceptor must be sought before any pious act, including gifts of kine.
shots.B13C168S75H05: Footnote 358 explains that in Yoga or samadhi the sense of the body is lost, and the felicity of Brahma is glimpsed.
shots.B13C168S76H01: Footnote 359 explains govritti as the cow's habit of not storing for the morrow, and so describes one who stores nothing.
shots.B13C168S76H02: Footnote 360 links the gift of a cow to the Brahmana in verse 25 and the elaboration in verse 26.
shots.B13C168S76H03: Footnote 361 says children born of a Homa, without women, were thought to merit gifts of kine, while the usual birth is also meant.
shots.B13C168S76H04: Footnote 362 says the cow should be given while she still gives milk and her calf is unweaned.
shots.B13C168S76H05: Footnote 363 says the Bombay reading kshanene is correct, and the other reading makes almost no sense.
shots.B13C168S77H01: Footnote 364 says vikrayartham may mean killing for sale, though the phrase seems redundant.
shots.B13C168S77H02: Footnote 365 distinguishes vows, which involve positive worship, from observances, which involve only abstention.
shots.B13C168S77H03: Footnote 366 says the orthodox believe rituals are eternal, existing before they were written down.
shots.B13C168S77H04: Footnote 367 glosses swah and the red cow, and notes the Vedic terms and the mantras used in giving cows.
shots.B13C168S77H05: Footnote 368 explains that a gift of a cow earns its merit at the eighth step of the recipient's journey home, and that the cow's milk serves his home rites.
shots.B13C168S78H01: Footnote 369 describes Ashtami, the eighth lunar day, when cows are worshipped with sandal, vermilion and wreaths.
shots.B13C168S78H02: Footnote 370 says sikhi means a bull, named for the hump it carries.
shots.B13C168S78H03: Footnote 371 describes a Kapila cow as one that gives plenty of milk and has other virtues.
shots.B13C168S78H04: Footnote 372 says there can be no sacrifice without ghee, which is made from milk.
shots.B13C168S78H05: Footnote 373 explains uchchhishta as the remnant after a meal, and says milk from the udders is not impure.
shots.B13C168S79H01: Footnote 374 says swastayana is a rite of propitiation that brings blessing and removes misery.
shots.B13C168S79H02: Footnote 375 explains a wet cowhide as one dipped in water to be purified, and the prosperity that kine confer.
shots.B13C168S79H03: Footnote 376 says the first line of verse 4 connects with verse 3, and that immobile creatures cannot give away cows.
shots.B13C168S79H04: Footnote 377 defines vallaki as the Indian lute and nupura as an anklet ornament.
shots.B13C168S79H05: Footnote 378 says bhumidah means giver of land, a name King Saudasa earned by gifts of land to Brahmanas.
shots.B13C168S80H01: Footnote 379 gives names for the cow, linked to the plough, beauty, the origin of all things, and motherhood.
shots.B13C168S80H02: Footnote 380 says ghee is sacred because it is used in sacrifice, and that it is both sacred and cleansing.
shots.B13C168S80H03: Footnote 381 identifies Sri as the goddess of Prosperity and says Bhishma's answer will explain the question.
shots.B13C168S80H04: Footnote 382 says Devendreshu is a misreading of Daitendreshu.
shots.B13C168S80H05: Footnote 383 says giving gold is taken as giving the whole universe.
shots.B13C168S81H01: Footnote 384 says the phrase means water, which is identical with Agni.
shots.B13C168S81H02: Footnote 385 explains fire-making by rubbing two sticks of Sami, a very inflammable wood used in rites.
shots.B13C168S81H03: Footnote 386 explains hiranyaretas as having gold for his vital seed.
shots.B13C168S81H04: Footnote 387 explains Vasumati as the earth that received Agni's golden seed, the highest wealth.
shots.B13C168S81H05: Footnote 388 derives Skanda's name from skanna, fallen out, and Guha from his hidden birth in the wilderness.
shots.B13C168S82H01: Footnote 389 explains jatarupa as the excellent form Agni took after his birth.
shots.B13C168S82H02: Footnote 390 quotes the commentator that the moving world was made for active life.
shots.B13C168S82H03: Footnote 391 says sattwa is identified with buddhi, which like light discovers all things, and is all-pervading.
shots.B13C168S82H05: Footnote 393 says these are different names of Brahman and Mahadeva.
shots.B13C168S83H01: Footnote 394 says 'hence' refers to the identity of Agni with Brahman and Rudra, not to the line just before.
shots.B13C168S83H02: Footnote 395 explains pravartakam as leading to righteous acts and purity of mind.
shots.B13C168S83H03: Footnote 396 says the Pitris are worshipped on the new moon and the gods on the first lighted day, with the Sraddha first on other days.
shots.B13C168S83H04: Footnote 397 says anwaharyam means performed afterwards, and that the new-moon afternoon Sraddha must precede the worship of the gods.
shots.B13C168S83H05: Footnote 398 identifies masha as the pulse Phascolus Roxburghii.
shots.B13C168S84H01: Footnote 399 says vadhrinasa may mean a large bull, a bird or a goat, most likely a bull.
shots.B13C168S84H02: Footnote 400 explains pitrikshaye as the day of the dead, and identifies kalasaka and lauham.
shots.B13C168S84H03: Footnote 401 notes the sanctity of Gaya, where Sraddhas are performed under the Akshaya banian.
shots.B13C168S84H04: Footnote 402 explains nitya acts as obligatory and kamya acts as optional.
shots.B13C168S84H05: Footnote 403 explains the phrase as setting a body of kings in motion, that is, becoming an overlord.
shots.B13C168S85H01: Footnote 404 explains that Brahmanas stained with vice are kept out of the feeding line, a kind of outlawry.
shots.B13C168S85H02: Footnote 405 says the term refers to those who have undergone natural circumcision.
shots.B13C168S85H03: Footnote 406 says the term implies soothsayers.
shots.B13C168S85H04: Footnote 407 says libations poured on ashes bring no merit, since only blazing Agni carries them to their targets.
shots.B13C168S85H05: Footnote 408 explains the simile of a bird leaving its perch as the fall from heaven, which the translator finds far-fetched.
shots.B13C168S86H01: Footnote 409 criticises the vernacular versions for careless errors and explains the phrase about the one who has not sown.
shots.B13C168S86H02: Footnote 410 says a calumniator, his sire and his son meet with ruin from such an act.
shots.B13C168S86H03: Footnote 411 describes the purificatory rites after mourning: shaving, bathing and wearing new clothes.
shots.B13C168S86H04: Footnote 412 explains that the father does for the son what sons ordinarily do for their fathers.
shots.B13C168S86H05: Footnote 413 notes that one vernacular version reads the wrong word kshama for akshaya.
shots.B13C168S87H01: Footnote 414 says Ravana and other Rakshasas of Pulastya's line are known as Brahma-Rakshasas.
shots.B13C168S87H02: Footnote 415 says a fast that mortifies the body is not penance, and may be sinful.
shots.B13C168S87H03: Footnote 416 explains upavasa as abstaining from food between the two meal times, not bodily mortification.
shots.B13C168S87H04: Footnote 417 says meat from sacrificial animals is allowed and does not make a man an eater of meat.
shots.B13C168S87H05: Footnote 418 explains prashthauhi as a cow carrying her second calf and grishti as one that has borne only her first.
shots.B13C168S88H01: Footnote 419 says the instruction to learn the Rishis' names was meant to warn the Rakshasi.
shots.B13C168S88H02: Footnote 420 says Vasishtha attributes the leanness of himself and his companions to neglect of daily rites.
shots.B13C168S88H03: Footnote 421 notes that lotus stalks are eaten in India and count as heavy food.
shots.B13C168S88H04: Footnote 422 explains Sunahsakha as a friend of dogs, named for the dog a newcomer kept.
shots.B13C168S88H05: Footnote 423 explains brahma-danda as the Brahmana's curse, which can blast even the unborn, unlike Indra's thunderbolt.
shots.B13C168S89H01: Footnote 424 says libations on straw fires are wasted, as if poured on ashes.
shots.B13C168S89H02: Footnote 425 notes the old aversion to living on a wife's family, and that returned hospitality is seen as mean and harmful to merit.
shots.B13C168S89H03: Footnote 426 explains a genitive form and says a Brahmana woman who bears a warlike son is a reproach.
shots.B13C168S89H04: Footnote 427 says righteousness declines with the ages, from whole in the Krita age to a quarter in Kali.
shots.B13C168S89H05: Footnote 428 says the Rishis held the class distinctions eternal and regarded equality of men as an evil.
shots.B13C168S90H01: Footnote 429 says forgiveness is the Brahmana's duty, and that retaliation and eating marrow flesh are grave faults.
shots.B13C168S90H02: Footnote 430 says a religious mendicant should wander and sleep where night overtakes him, and not stay in towns.
shots.B13C168S90H03: Footnote 431 says tilling the soil is a transgression for a Brahmana.
shots.B13C168S90H04: Footnote 432 says good food should be shared with children and servants.
shots.B13C168S90H05: Footnote 433 says a Brahmana should leave a village whose only well is used by all classes.
shots.B13C168S91H01: Footnote 434 says penance belongs in the woods, and that performing it on village roads to win gifts is a grave fault.
shots.B13C168S91H02: Footnote 435 describes cruel milking practices, the sinfulness of using another cow's calf, and the unfitness of milk held in white brass.
shots.B13C168S91H03: Footnote 436 says the discourse is eternal because its subject, duty, is eternal.
shots.B13C168S91H04: Footnote 437 explains sastra as anything that governs conduct, so the list of duties is a sastra.
shots.B13C168S91H05: Footnote 438 explains the term for dog-keepers as members of the lowest caste.
shots.B13C168S92H01: Footnote 439 takes tapah as the duties of the four orders and dharma as compassion and similar virtues.
shots.B13C168S92H02: Footnote 440 explains dhupas as incenses made to burn slowly, a regular part of worship of the deities.
shots.B13C168S92H03: Footnote 441 notes that tejas may mean beauty or fame here, though its usual sense of energy need not be dropped.
shots.B13C168S92H04: Footnote 442 says those who die while the sun moves south are dragged through darkness, and lamps help them avoid it.
shots.B13C168S92H05: Footnote 443 says the juice of deciduous herbs means oils of mustard seed and castor seed.
shots.B13C168S93H01: Footnote 444 says well-fried paddy, powdered, is sometimes used to coat meat dishes.
shots.B13C168S93H02: Footnote 445 says the only punishment in the Krita age was to cry 'fie' at an offender.
shots.B13C168S93H03: Footnote 446 notes a variant, vatsakah for utsavah, and says such rites promote children's welfare.
shots.B13C168S93H04: Footnote 447 says some texts read grahaya for dwijaya, meaning guests.
shots.B13C168S93H05: Footnote 448 says a giver of lights gains beauty and strength for as many years as the instants the lights burn.
shots.B13C168S94H01: Footnote 449 says kshatrabandhu means a low or vile Kshatriya.
shots.B13C168S94H02: Footnote 450 gives the literal sense: why do you dip parts of your body into a pond?
shots.B13C168S94H03: Footnote 451 says study of the Vedas equals gifts in merit, so gifts of goods are called gifts of other kinds.
shots.B13C168S94H04: Footnote 452 says friendship is seven-word, meaning that exchanging seven words or walking seven steps makes friends.
shots.B13C168S94H05: Footnote 453 says the Bombay text reads Somapithi, a drinker of sacrificial soma.
shots.B13C168S95H01: Footnote 454 explains the Ekaratra, Pancharatra and Ekadasaratra sacrifices as fasts and gifts of one, five and eleven nights.
shots.B13C168S95H02: Footnote 455 describes the golden moon ornaments worn by ladies on the forehead and at the waist.
shots.B13C168S95H03: Footnote 456 explains how in ancient times kings placed sacrificial altars by throwing a sami log to mark each site.
shots.B13C168S95H04: Footnote 457 says a sinful man who mends his conduct wards off the evils his sins would bring.
shots.B13C168S95H05: Footnote 458 describes idle habits such as crumbling earth, tearing grass and biting the nails.
shots.B13C168S96H01: Footnote 459 says the Brahma Muhurta is the time when the sun is just below the horizon.
shots.B13C168S96H02: Footnote 460 says the morning and evening prayers are called adoring the two twilights.
shots.B13C168S96H03: Footnote 461 explains the vow of Brahmacharya as abstaining from sex except with one's wife in her season.
shots.B13C168S96H04: Footnote 462 says the Bombay text reads the second line differently, and that the wounds of harsh words fester.
shots.B13C168S96H05: Footnote 463 describes the foods samyava, krisara, sashkuli and payasa.
shots.B13C168S97H01: Footnote 464 says one should examine the bed by lamplight before lying down, since antarddhane means in darkness.
shots.B13C168S97H02: Footnote 465 explains pranan as the upper openings of the body, such as nostrils, ears and eyes.
shots.B13C168S97H03: Footnote 466 says a Brahmana is more powerful than the other two classes, since he can harm an enemy he cannot see.
shots.B13C168S97H04: Footnote 467 describes the custom of wearing a single flower in the coronal lock.
shots.B13C168S97H05: Footnote 468 says dry perfumes should not be used, but those pounded with water into a paste.
shots.B13C168S98H01: Footnote 469 describes the fringes of a Hindu's cloth, which have fewer threads than the body of the cloth.
shots.B13C168S98H02: Footnote 470 says Hinduism is a vast system of personal hygiene, and that rigid Hindus still observe these rules on dress.
shots.B13C168S98H03: Footnote 471 gives botanical names for priyangu, vilwa, tagara and kesara.
shots.B13C168S98H04: Footnote 472 says na is the nominative of nri, meaning man.
shots.B13C168S98H05: Footnote 473 says one translation takes valena as child and para-sraddha as the first Sraddha.
shots.B13C168S99H01: Footnote 474 says the noise refers to chewing, sucking or licking, an ugly habit.
shots.B13C168S99H02: Footnote 475 says doubt about food refers to whether it can be digested, is clean, or is too much.
shots.B13C168S99H03: Footnote 476 says that at a Sraddha certain articles are placed on part of the right hand before being offered.
shots.B13C168S99H04: Footnote 477 explains achamana as washing after a meal, but at the start of rites only touching the lips and parts with water.
shots.B13C168S99H05: Footnote 478 says a Brahmana's aid is needed to choose a site, set the house's directions, and fix the day to build.
shots.B13C168S100H01: Footnote 479 follows Nilakantha in reading the verse as a ban on killing birds at night, and discusses the word dwija.
shots.B13C168S100H02: Footnote 480 says pravaras show the race of a man through the names of Vedic Rishis.
shots.B13C168S100H03: Footnote 481 says ayonim means of unknown birth, and viyonim of mean birth.
shots.B13C168S100H04: Footnote 482 says Brahmanih refers to the Vedic rituals, not to persons of the first order.
shots.B13C168S100H05: Footnote 483 says one must bathe after a shave and remains impure until doing so.
shots.B13C168S101H01: Footnote 484 says uddesa means in brief.
shots.B13C168S101H02: Footnote 485 says acharah covers one's conduct toward all beings and includes the sentiments one holds.
shots.B13C168S101H03: Footnote 486 says the flower of the cane cannot be plucked for offering to the deities.
shots.B13C168S101H04: Footnote 487 ranks the teachers: the Acharya, then the Upadhyaya, then the father, and the mother, who equals the whole earth.
shots.B13C168S101H05: Footnote 488 compares the verses with Manu and notes that birth from the teacher is the true, immortal birth.
shots.B13C168S102H01: Footnote 489 describes the kanchi as a waist ornament and the nupura as a silver anklet with small bells.
shots.B13C168S102H02: Footnote 490 glosses avaguna as nirguna, and ekatma and asamhta as alone and helpless.
shots.B13C168S102H03: Footnote 491 explains that a padma is a very large number, rendered as millions upon millions of years.
shots.B13C168S102H04: Footnote 492 works out the year count from the arrows and fires, adding sixteen and thirty-five to reach fifty-one.
shots.B13C168S102H05: Footnote 493 says the number is a countless one, almost.
shots.B13C168S103H01: Footnote 494 says the exact number of years is not stated here.
shots.B13C168S103H02: Footnote 495 says some beautiful women have been dark, citing Draupadi, called Krishna, and the Syama women.
shots.B13C168S103H03: Footnote 496 says the figure given is very large.
shots.B13C168S103H04: Footnote 497 says this sacrifice involved the slaughter of a human being.
shots.B13C168S103H05: Footnote 498 says the exact years given are a fabulous figure.
shots.B13C168S104H01: Footnote 499 explains abhravakasasila as having the attribute of the open sky, pure as ether.
shots.B13C168S104H02: Footnote 500 says sacrifices have as their soul either the rites or the fasts, which are of equal merit.
shots.B13C168S104H03: Footnote 501 says a tirtha is a sacred water, but Bhishma takes the word in a different sense.
shots.B13C168S104H04: Footnote 502 says the lake Manasa here stands for the Soul, fathomless and pure, with Truth for its waters.
shots.B13C168S104H05: Footnote 503 says being freed from 'mine' means identifying oneself with all creatures.
shots.B13C168S105H01: Footnote 504 says such a man's merit frees his ancestors and descendants from misery in the next world.
shots.B13C168S105H02: Footnote 505 says that in the Naramedha a human being was offered as sacrifice.
shots.B13C168S105H03: Footnote 506 says the unlearned act for the body and the senses, which are the not-self.
shots.B13C168S105H04: Footnote 507 explains nichayam as remaining firm.
shots.B13C168S105H05: Footnote 508 says that when the soul leaves the body it is accompanied by Righteousness.
shots.B13C168S106H01: Footnote 509 says the intermediate beings, between gods and men, are animals and birds.
shots.B13C168S106H02: Footnote 510 explains Brahma-Rakshasas as Rakshasas born into the Brahmana order, like Ravana.
shots.B13C168S106H03: Footnote 511 gives botanical names for pulses and grains such as masha, kulatta, kalaya, mudga and atasi.
shots.B13C168S106H04: Footnote 512 says a kanka is a bird of prey.
shots.B13C168S106H05: Footnote 513 describes the torments of hell: beating, impaling, fiery vessels, blades, heated sand, and salmali thorns.
shots.B13C168S107H01: Footnote 514 identifies nishpava with rajamasha, a bean, and halagolaka as a long-tailed worm.
shots.B13C168S107H02: Footnote 515 identifies the krikara as a partridge and the vartaka as a quail.
shots.B13C168S107H03: Footnote 516 says tailapayin, meaning oil-drinker, is a name for the cockroach.
shots.B13C168S107H04: Footnote 517 says vyathitah and vyadhitah are the correct readings.
shots.B13C168S107H05: Footnote 518 says a day is lost when no gift of food is made on it.
shots.B13C168S108H01: Footnote 519 says the particle cha implies cupidity along with anger, and faults the Burdwan rendering of the verse.
shots.B13C168S108H02: A heading in the text reads The Mahabharata.
shots.B13C168S108H03: Footnote 520 says the man leaves no trace since he is identified with Brahma, unlike the deities, who seek fixed abodes.
shots.B13C168S108H04: Footnote 521 gives the rule of asking oneself how one would feel if refused, applied to every kind of request.
shots.B13C168S108H05: Footnote 522 says killing, inciting killing, and planning it in the mind all make a person guilty.
shots.B13C168S109H01: Footnote 523 says eating meat builds a taste for it, so total abstinence is the best course.
shots.B13C168S109H02: Footnote 524 says the assurance of harmlessness is the Dakshina of the great sacrifice of compassion.
shots.B13C168S109H03: Footnote 525 gives the etymology of mansa, flesh, as the meat that says: he eats me, so I shall eat him.
shots.B13C168S109H04: Footnote 526 explains that injury done in one life brings its consequences in the next, such as rebirth as a tiger.
shots.B13C168S109H05: Footnote 527 says a worm can recall its past life because of the merit of seeing the sage.
shots.B13C168S110H01: Footnote 528 says human beings enjoy the fruits of their good acts and endure those of their evil acts.
shots.B13C168S110H02: Footnote 529 says a creature without speech has been forsaken by everything and is in great misery.
shots.B13C168S110H03: Footnote 530 gives a paraphrase: a feeling of disgust arose.
shots.B13C168S110H04: Footnote 531 identifies the Swairini family with the Munis, and the Ajnata-charitam phrase with Krishna-Dwaipayana.
shots.B13C168S110H05: Footnote 532 says prithagatman means a soul still bound by its vestments, and sukhatman one who has passed beyond them.
shots.B13C168S111H01: Footnote 533 says a palmful of water given to the deserving may win what a hundred sacrifices win, which the translator finds surprising.
shots.B13C168S111H02: Footnote 534 says those who pursue carnal pleasures meet with misery, and those who practise austerity find felicity.
shots.B13C168S111H03: Footnote 535 says the sight of the Lord is the reward of one's own acts and brings prosperity through his kindness.
shots.B13C168S111H04: Footnote 536 says an ascetic at any stage and a man who is omniscient are regarded as equal.
shots.B13C168S111H05: Footnote 537 says the desired object can never be reached, and that is why the speaker is pale and lean.
shots.B13C168S112H01: Footnote 538 says a blameless person can still be cursed, and that the anxiety this causes explains the listener's pallor.
shots.B13C168S112H02: Footnote 539 says the phrase yamena praptam means reached by Yama, as the commentator explains.
shots.B13C168S112H03: Footnote 540 ranks the sin of taking gifts: a butcher counts as one unit, an oilman as ten, a petty chief as ten thousand, and a great king as five thousand.
shots.B13C168S112H04: Footnote 541 says the rule rests on the declarations of the scriptures.
shots.B13C168S112H05: Footnote 542 says a Brahmana who acts as priest and eats at a Sraddha becomes the Pitri of the host, and so must abstain from his wife that day or commit adultery.
shots.B13C168S113H01: Footnote 543 explains batakashaya as a substance made by pounding banyan aerial roots, identifies priyangu with Brassica juncea, and says shashtika paddy ripens in sixty days.
shots.B13C168S113H02: Footnote 544 says libations from men who do not tend their fire daily are not carried by the fire to their destined places.
shots.B13C168S113H03: Footnote 545 says kshirapah means those who live on milk, that is, little children.
shots.B13C168S113H04: Footnote 546 says the aurddhadehika gift is one made at Sraddhas and similar rites to better the state of the dead.
shots.B13C168S113H05: Footnote 547 says the gift of lamps means lighting lamps in the sky, set on poles fastened to the tallest trees.
shots.B13C168S114H01: Footnote 548 says that at evening one should salute one's own feet, a custom the translator thinks has died out in Bengal, and notes the old offering to a whirl of fresh cowdung.
shots.B13C168S114H02: Footnote 549 calls the second line unintelligible and prefers the reading sraddheshu to schidreshu.
shots.B13C168S114H03: Footnote 550 says vows and fasts need a formal resolve stating the purpose and the act, since even a bath in holy water yields no merit without it.
shots.B13C168S114H04: Footnote 551 says vrishalipati means husband of a Sudra woman, and that marrying the lowest class, marrying before an elder brother, or marrying a grown girl can earn the name.
shots.B13C168S114H05: Footnote 552 says kutapa is the hour about noon, and that a Sraddha done when the elephant's shadow falls brings the merit of thirteen years of Sraddhas.
shots.B13C168S115H01: Footnote 553 describes the Indian toothbrush as a twig with one end chewed into fibres, used once and then thrown away.
shots.B13C168S115H02: Footnote 554 says it is hard to identify the plants karanjaka and suvarachala.
shots.B13C168S115H03: Footnote 555 lists broken copper and brass vessels, broken bedsteads, cocks and dogs, and tree roots as sources of quarrel, loss or danger in a house.
shots.B13C168S115H04: Footnote 556 says a Sudra must never kindle a Brahmana's fire, and women should not help arrange the offerings at Sraddhas.
shots.B13C168S115H05: Footnote 557 says the Pramathas are ghostly companions of Mahadeva, and that their name means smiters.
shots.B13C168S116H01: Footnote 558 explains anujnatah as permitted, and tells how Brahman asked Maheswara to accept kine, after which the bull became his emblem.
shots.B13C168S116H02: Footnote 559 says sambhrama may mean joy shown as horripilation, or else alacrity.
shots.B13C168S116H03: Footnote 560 says upavasa here means the subjugation of the senses.
shots.B13C168S116H04: Footnote 561 says a man who eats at proper hours keeps the fast, and one who keeps to his wife in her season observes chastity.
shots.B13C168S116H05: Footnote 562 says to sell the Vedas or any knowledge is a great sin.
shots.B13C168S117H01: Footnote 563 gives the reading nabaram natirogratah and says the thing described includes all, as comprehensive as Brahman.
shots.B13C168S117H02: Footnote 564 describes three kinds of sages: those who wash all their vessels daily, those who husk grain with two stones, and those who husk it with their teeth.
shots.B13C168S117H03: Footnote 565 says swasarirapa-jivishu means those who need no one's help to keep their bodies alive.
shots.B13C168S117H04: Footnote 566 says the great forests are called Virasthana because cowards cannot enter or live in them.
shots.B13C168S117H05: Footnote 567 says marum samsadhya means giving up even air and water as food.
shots.B13C168S118H01: Footnote 568 says vira here means heroes of righteousness and penance rather than warriors, and that virasana is a seat for yogins.
shots.B13C168S118H02: Footnote 569 says nisargat means by original creation or birth, through the Self-born.
shots.B13C168S118H03: Footnote 570 takes ugra as a fierce person or a hunter of mixed caste, and says a good Brahmana should refuse the food such men supply.
shots.B13C168S118H04: Footnote 571 says a Brahmana who dies with the food of a lower order in his body, or who lives on it, is reborn in that order.
shots.B13C168S118H05: Footnote 572 says kundasin means a pander, or one who eats from the cooking vessel instead of plates or leaves.
shots.B13C168S119H01: Footnote 573 says a Vaisya becomes a Brahmana by keeping the duties of verses 30 to 33, and becomes a great Kshatriya on the way.
shots.B13C168S119H02: Footnote 574 says the phrase may also mean taking a sixth share of the merit that subjects earn by righteous acts.
shots.B13C168S119H03: Footnote 575 says an inferior must stand aside for a superior, with Kshatriyas giving way to Brahmanas, Vaisyas to Kshatriyas, and Sudras to Vaisyas.
shots.B13C168S119H04: Footnote 576 glosses the pair as soul, including the Supreme Soul, and not-soul.
shots.B13C168S119H05: Footnote 577 says Gauri is another name for the earth.
shots.B13C168S120H01: Footnote 578 says rivers are feminine, though the Indus is an exception, and that tirthas are places with sacred waters.
shots.B13C168S120H02: Footnote 579 says a man free of vanity deserves the name Purusha, and that the lady's question is a compliment, since females follow their nature.
shots.B13C168S120H03: Footnote 580 says sindhu here means a river in general, not the Indus, and that devika is another name of the Sarayu.
shots.B13C168S120H04: Footnote 581 says that in Hindu scripture marriage is not a contract but the union of two into one for the better performance of pious acts.
shots.B13C168S120H05: Footnote 582 explains Trivikrama as Vishnu, who covered the three worlds in three steps when he took the form of a dwarf to beguile Vali.
shots.B13C168S121H01: Footnote 583 says the speakers, unlike the Lord who holds all knowledge within, are light-minded, and let out a secret to one who will laugh at their pride.
shots.B13C168S121H02: Footnote 584 says no one wishes to be beaten by another except a son, so the Rishis wish Krishna a son greater than himself.
shots.B13C168S121H03: Footnote 585 says pushti means growth or advancement, and so stands generally for excellence and greatness.
shots.B13C168S121H04: Footnote 586 says the correct reading is pratisravam, meaning promise, not pratisrayam.
shots.B13C168S121H05: Footnote 587 says the pledge probably refers to the oaths Bhima and others made about slaying the Kauravas.
shots.B13C168S122H01: Footnote 588 says a king earns great merit by using the rod of chastisement properly, which keeps subjects within the bounds of duty.
shots.B13C168S122H02: Footnote 589 identifies Vasudeva with Narayana and Arjuna with Nara, who did penance at Vadari, which Vyasa later made his retreat.
shots.B13C168S122H03: Footnote 590 says the sages do not speculate on the original creation, only on the creation that follows Brahman's waking, since eternity has no beginning.
shots.B13C168S122H04: Footnote 591 glosses putatman as the cleansed soul, purusha as one who lies in the body, sakshi as the witness, and kshetrajna as the knower of the body.
shots.B13C168S122H05: Footnote 592 glosses yoga, pradhana as Nature in the Sankhya system, and Narasinghavapu as the lion-headed form that slew Hiranyakasipu.
shots.B13C168S123H01: Footnote 593 explains sarva as the source of all things, sambhava as one who takes birth at will, and bhuvana as one who assigns the fruits of acts.
shots.B13C168S123H02: Footnote 594 explains sambhu as one whose birth is self-willed, notes that the Adityas are twelve, and glosses dhatri.
shots.B13C168S123H03: Footnote 595 explains aprameya as beyond the senses and inference, gives two senses of Hrishikesa and Sankara's solar and lunar reading, and glosses manu as mantra.
shots.B13C168S123H04: Footnote 596 explains Krishna as one always in joy, glosses Lohitaksha, Pratardana and Prabhuta, and takes Pavitram, Mangalam and Param as one name.
shots.B13C168S123H05: Footnote 597 gives three senses of Pranada, explains Prana, names Hiranyagarbha as the Grandsire, and explains Bhugarbha as one who has the earth for his abdomen.
shots.B13C168S124H01: Footnote 598 says the Supreme is pure soul, resting on its own essence without needing gods or men.
shots.B13C168S124H02: Footnote 599 explains aha as the day on which the soul is awakened, samvatsara as Time's essence, and vyala as a huge and fierce snake.
shots.B13C168S124H03: Footnote 600 gives Valadeva Vidyabhushan's reading of vrishakapi as one who showers blessings and makes foes tremble.
shots.B13C168S124H04: Footnote 601 says Vishnu is placed within Sisumara, the Northern Bear, round which the stars seem to revolve.
shots.B13C168S124H05: Footnote 602 says one should not worship the deities on a full stomach, and should abstain from food and drink for formal worship.
shots.B13C168S125H01: Footnote 603 tells how Rama of Bhrigu's race quarrelled with Kumara, won his battle-axe from Siva, and destroyed the Kshatriyas twenty-one times.
shots.B13C168S125H02: Footnote 604 says many words beginning with Mahat echo Krishna's own words in the Gita.
shots.B13C168S125H03: Footnote 605 refers to Hanumat and the other apes that Rama led against Ravana.
shots.B13C168S125H04: Footnote 606 says the universe is made of soul and not-soul, and that the jiva in ignorance takes the body for the self until true knowledge comes.
shots.B13C168S125H05: Footnote 607 says untimely deaths do not occur in such places, nor fear of oppression or unjust punishment by the king.
shots.B13C168S126H01: Footnote 608 says the Bengal reading mrishtascha varina is wrong and the Bombay reading mrishtasya varinsha is right.
shots.B13C168S126H02: Footnote 609 says kavi here means Agni, and that one vernacular translator wrongly takes it for the teacher Sukra.
shots.B13C168S126H03: Footnote 610 calls the last verse, as the Bengal texts read it, faulty, and gives nastyandam astitu brahma as the correct reading.
shots.B13C168S126H04: Footnote 611 says that to an afflicted person the day seems long.
shots.B13C168S126H05: Footnote 612 says Kesava upholds righteousness when it is in danger, as in the Gita, and does not dispel every moral doubt.
shots.B13C168S127H01: Footnote 613 refers to the existence of Brahma when nothing else is.
shots.B13C168S127H02: Footnote 614 explains the fivefold seed as the four orders of creatures together with the acts that determine the condition of all beings.
shots.B13C168S127H03: Footnote 615 identifies the tree as the bael, Aegle marmelos.
shots.B13C168S127H04: Footnote 616 says Durvasa is a portion of Mahadeva, so Yudhishthira's question really concerns Mahadeva.
shots.B13C168S127H05: Footnote 617 explains parvam as a knot, and salya as the space between two knots in reeds and bamboos.
shots.B13C168S128H01: Footnote 618 says the allusion is to the fiery mare's head said to wander through the ocean.
shots.B13C168S128H02: Footnote 619 says verses four to nine are very difficult, sets out the commentator's readings on perception, scripture, theories of creation, Yoga, the mendicant and the Vedic words, and says the Burdwan pundits garbled the passage.
shots.B13C168S128H03: Footnote 620 says the three sources of knowledge, perception, inference and good conduct, are fallible, so the only remaining standard is the hearing of the scriptures.
shots.B13C168S128H04: Footnote 621 says the atripyantah are seekers after the right, who like Yudhishthira are anxious about what they should do.
shots.B13C168S128H05: Footnote 622 names the five who must be fed first: the deities, the Pitris, guests, the various creatures, and relatives.
shots.B13C168S129H01: Footnote 623 notes that some texts read nabhibhavet, meaning one should not overpower an old man.
shots.B13C168S129H02: Footnote 624 says the custom of blessing a person who sneezes is very old and widespread, and still found among Hindus.
shots.B13C168S129H03: Footnote 625 says confessing a sin before the wise lightens it, while concealing it after the act marks a confirmed sinner.
shots.B13C168S129H04: Footnote 626 says 'covered by righteousness' describes a sinner who has stumbled, restrains himself, and turns to righteous acts.
shots.B13C168S129H05: Footnote 627 says the state of every creature is set by acts and nature, so that good or ill fortune, and the poor learned or rich ignorant man, must be ascribed to these two causes.
shots.B13C168S130H01: Footnote 628 says a man becomes righteous by doing righteous acts himself or by inducing others to do them, and unrighteous in the same way.
shots.B13C168S130H02: Footnote 629 says righteousness leads to regions of felicity, the first being eternal and the rewards not, and raises the question why the effect is not eternal when the cause is.
shots.B13C168S130H03: Footnote 630 separates nishkama righteousness, which leads to Brahma, from sakama righteousness, which leads to heaven, and says kala means sankalpa, so dhruvahkalah is nishkama dharma.
shots.B13C168S130H04: Footnote 631 says calah means sankalpa here.
shots.B13C168S130H05: The running heading names the work as the Mahabharata.
shots.B13C168S131H01: The colophon word 'of' links the title to the name of the author.
shots.B13C168S131H02: The colophon names the author as Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa.
shots.B13C168S27H01: Footnote 114 explains Mahadeva's defeat by Krishna at Vana as a mark of his favour, since Krishna broke his vow against bearing arms at Kurukshetra to honour Bhishma's vow.
shots.B13C168S27H02: Footnote 115 says that at universal dissolution, when all is a vast expanse of water, a banyan appears where the immortal Markandeya sees a boy who is Mahavishnu.
shots.B13C168S27H03: Footnote 116 offers another sense: you are he at whose approach the Daitya hosts fled in every direction.
shots.B13C168S27H04: Footnote 117 says the phrase means that you are Time itself.
